title: Singing Waheguru
hookLine: the simplest kirtan is singing Waheguru to a simple tune

cards: Go back to the second day of this whole path. The word was Waheguru, and the line was just: wow. Wonder, plus teacher.
The wonderful Guru. Now picture the end of a long evening program at a gurdwara. The shabads are done.
The harmonium player starts a slow, simple tune, four or five notes going round, and the whole room begins to sing one word. Waheguru. Waheguru.
Grandparents, teenagers, tired kids leaning on their parents. Nobody needs a screen. Nobody needs to read Gurmukhi.

teach.b: Singing Waheguru is the simplest kirtan there is: one word, one tune, sung again and again. Sikhs often call it Waheguru simran, remembering God by singing the name. Waheguru has a special place in Sikh life.
Sikhs call it the gurmantar, the Guru's own word to repeat; the early Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas wrote of it as that word.
And near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, poets at the Gurus' court, known as the Bhatts, sing it over and over in praise of the Guru.
It's what Sikhs say when they greet each other in the Khalsa way, what they whisper when they wake, what they say when they're amazed or afraid. Singing it does something saying it doesn't.

teach.h: THE TUNE SLOWS THE WORD DOWN.
teach.b: The tune slows the word down. Wah, the wonder, gets to open all the way. Guru, the teacher who leads from dark to light, lands softly at the end.
The repeating stops being boring and starts being steady, like waves.
After a few rounds you're not thinking about the word; you're inside it. That's the point of simran: not to think about God, but to remember, with the whole self. There's no one correct tune.
Every gurdwara, every family, seems to have its own. Some are slow and low, almost a lullaby; some pick up speed until the whole room is swaying.
The tune serves the name. If you only ever learn one piece of kirtan, many Sikhs would say, let it be this. It fits in any voice, any room, any day.

how: Sikh congregations often sing Waheguru simran together, a single word repeated to a simple tune, and many Sikhs repeat Waheguru through the day, sung, spoken or silently.

games.q: you're at the end of an evening program. the harmonium starts a slow tune and the room begins to sing. you don't read Gurmukhi. what can you do?
o: stay silent; it's for people who know the words.
join in: there's only one word, Waheguru.
look for a translation on your phone.
games.why: Waheguru simran has one word, so everyone can join, whatever they can read.

practice: Softly sing Waheguru five times to any simple tune, two or three notes is plenty, or put the word into yesterday's hum: let the wah open like a surprise, and the Guru settle. If singing feels like too much, hum it or whisper it.
After the fifth, stay quiet and listen to the room, and if you'd like, sing it five times more.
